title: CF Industries Case
text: CF created value by controlling the supply chain, storage, and pricing information for fertilizer, using regulatory barriers to capture market advantage.

title: CF Industries Case
text:
- CF created value by having ammonia where and when farmers needed it. ([[Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture#Case - CF Industries|Class 2 › Case - CF Industries]])
- CF captured value through terminals, which are heavily restricted by regulation (an entry barrier). ([[Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture#Case - CF Industries|Class 2 › Case - CF Industries]])
- Storage allowed CF to sell to the higher-priced agricultural market rather than the industrial market. ([[Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture#Case - CF Industries|Class 2 › Case - CF Industries]])
- The $3.8 billion expansion led competitors to cancel their own plans, acting as entry deterrence. ([[Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture#Case - CF Industries|Class 2 › Case - CF Industries]])

title: Cola Wars Case
text: The Cola Wars illustrates how Coke and Pepsi shaped competition by focusing on advertising and differentiation rather than price wars.

title: Cola Wars Case
text:
- Carbonated soft drinks represent 27% of US beverage consumption and $48 billion in US sales. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Case - Cola Wars|Class 4 › Case - Cola Wars]])
- Coke and Pepsi competed on advertising and marketing, moving competition from price to dimensions that grow the market. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Case - Cola Wars|Class 4 › Case - Cola Wars]])
- Entry barriers included scale in distribution, established channels, and brand recognition. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Case - Cola Wars|Class 4 › Case - Cola Wars]])

title: Intel Case
text: Intel's strategy shifted from DRAM to microprocessors, demonstrating how network effects and IP protection drive added value.

title: Intel Case
text:
- Intel's strategy in DRAM involved innovation and product design, being first to market, pricing high and moving on. ([[Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability#Case - Intel|Class 3 › Case - Intel]])
- Intel's added value in DRAM collapsed, but persisted in microprocessors because of network effects. ([[Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability#Case - Intel|Class 3 › Case - Intel]])
- Intel captured added value through Intel Inside and a systems business. ([[Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability#Case - Intel|Class 3 › Case - Intel]])

title: Moneyball Case
text: The Oakland A's found that on-base percentage predicted wins better than slugging, leading to an arbitrage opportunity that eventually converged toward market equilibrium.

title: Moneyball Case
text:
- Scouts valued players partly on looks (the "Good Face"). ([[Class 1 - Introduction to Strategy#Case - Moneyball|Class 1 › Case - Moneyball]])
- On-base percentage predicted wins better than slugging, yet sluggers were paid far more. ([[Class 1 - Introduction to Strategy#Case - Moneyball|Class 1 › Case - Moneyball]])
- The market price and the true value of OBP converged by about 2004-2005 as markets moved toward equilibrium. ([[Class 1 - Introduction to Strategy#Case - Moneyball|Class 1 › Case - Moneyball]])

title: Tesla Case
text: Tesla demonstrated how learning-curve and scale effects can overcome initial financial disadvantages, leveraging technological advantages to overcome high entry barriers.

title: Tesla Case
text:
- The Model S was Tesla's first real production car and the first entry by a new US carmaker since WWII. ([[Class 6 - Entry and Positioning#Case - Tesla|Class 6 › Case - Tesla]])
- Learning-curve and scale effects could make the numbers much better than they looked for a start-up. ([[Class 6 - Entry and Positioning#Case - Tesla|Class 6 › Case - Tesla]])
- Tesla overcame high barriers by building its brand and selling directly instead of through dealers. ([[Class 6 - Entry and Positioning#Case - Tesla|Class 6 › Case - Tesla]])
- Tesla's durable advantage may lie in software, batteries, and charging rather than car making. ([[Class 6 - Entry and Positioning#Case - Tesla|Class 6 › Case - Tesla]])

title: Dynamic Entry Games
text: This framework analyzes how incumbents will respond to an entrant's decision to enter, using backward induction to predict strategic responses.

id: vault/Entry and Competition/Dynamic Entry Games.md#Key Points#0
title: Dynamic Entry Games
text:
- The incumbent gets £69M if there is no entry, £60M if it accommodates and £34M if it retaliates. ([[Class 7 - Entry Dynamics#Dynamic entry games|Class 7 › Dynamic entry games]])
- The entrant enters if its fixed cost F is below £4.4M. ([[Class 7 - Entry Dynamics#Dynamic entry games|Class 7 › Dynamic entry games]])
- Having the extra option to expand makes the entrant worse off because it triggers retaliation. ([[Class 7 - Entry Dynamics#Dynamic entry games|Class 7 › Dynamic entry games]])

title: Entry and Exit
text: Entry and exit are common occurrences where entrants and exiting firms are generally smaller than established firms. Entry and exit rates vary significantly across different industries.

id: vault/Entry and Competition/Entry and Exit.md#Key Points#0
title: Entry and Exit
text:
- Entrants and exiting firms tend to be smaller than established firms. ([[Class 6 - Entry and Positioning#Facts about entry and exit|Class 6 › Facts about entry and exit]])
- Those that survive grow quickly. ([[Class 6 - Entry and Positioning#Facts about entry and exit|Class 6 › Facts about entry and exit]])
- Entry is broader than new firms, including new markets and new products. ([[Class 6 - Entry and Positioning#Facts about entry and exit|Class 6 › Facts about entry and exit]])
- Entry includes new markets (M-Pesa entering India, Amazon entering grocery) and new products (Ozempic, Vanilla Coke, the microprocessor). ([[Class 6 - Entry and Positioning#Facts about entry and exit|Class 6 › Facts about entry and exit]])

title: Entry Barriers
text: Barriers to entry make a market difficult to enter or less profitable for new competitors. These barriers can include economies of scale, scarce resources, and intellectual property.

title: Entry Barriers
text:
- Barriers include economies of scale relative to market size, scarce resources, and learning curves. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Entry and barriers to entry|Class 4 › Entry and barriers to entry]])
- Direct network effects and indirect platform network effects exist in the context of entry. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Entry and barriers to entry|Class 4 › Entry and barriers to entry]])
- Intellectual property, such as patents, is crucial in industries like pharmaceuticals. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Entry and barriers to entry|Class 4 › Entry and barriers to entry]])

title: Entry Deterrence
text: Incumbents can keep competitors out by changing the payoffs before entry occurs. This involves actions like limiting pricing or expanding capacity to make entry unattractive.

title: Entry Deterrence
text:
### From Class 7 - Entry Dynamics
- Limit pricing to make entry unattractive (Alcoa). ([[Class 7 - Entry Dynamics#Entry deterrence|Class 7 › Entry deterrence]])
- Capacity expansion to commit to fighting (DuPont in titanium dioxide, CF Industries). ([[Class 7 - Entry Dynamics#Entry deterrence|Class 7 › Entry deterrence]])
- Product proliferation to fill every niche so there is no room (cereal, drug variants, railroad branch lines). ([[Class 7 - Entry Dynamics#Entry deterrence|Class 7 › Entry deterrence]])
- Predatory pricing to build a reputation (OPEC, Uber, Walmart). ([[Class 7 - Entry Dynamics#Entry deterrence|Class 7 › Entry deterrence]])

### From Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions
- Large incumbents expand capacity to deter entrants. ([[Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions#Takeaways|Class 8 › Takeaways]])
- Lock large customers into long-term contracts. ([[Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions#Takeaways|Class 8 › Takeaways]])
- Punish small entrants to send a message. ([[Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions#Takeaways|Class 8 › Takeaways]])

title: Water Bottle Exercise
text: This exercise illustrates how positioning can influence outcomes when an entrant challenges an incumbent's offering.

id: vault/Entry and Competition/Water Bottle Exercise.md#Key Points#0
title: Water Bottle Exercise
text:
- A monopolist selling the insulated bottle at $20 to all 10 customers earns a profit of $100. ([[Class 6 - Entry and Positioning#Water bottle exercise|Class 6 › Water bottle exercise]])
- If the entrant copies the bottle at $19, the incumbent undercuts to $18.99, leading toward a price war. ([[Class 6 - Entry and Positioning#Water bottle exercise|Class 6 › Water bottle exercise]])
- To win back a few customers, the incumbent must lower its price to all of them. ([[Class 6 - Entry and Positioning#Water bottle exercise|Class 6 › Water bottle exercise]])
- Counter-positioning works better when the incumbent would find it hard to make your product well. ([[Class 6 - Entry and Positioning#Counter-positioning|Class 6 › Counter-positioning]])

title: Five Forces
text: Porter's Five Forces is a framework used to analyze how much value an industry can create and how much firms can keep as profit. It serves as a checklist to understand the context of competition.

title: Five Forces
text:
- The five forces are substitutes, buyer power, supplier power, entry, and rivalry. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Five Forces as a starting point|Class 4 › Five Forces as a starting point]])
- Substitutes meet the same need as your product and affect profit similarly to an entrant with a different product. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Substitutes|Class 4 › Substitutes]])
- Buyers can push prices down when they are few and large, when there are many substitutes, or when they can bypass the seller. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Buyer power and supplier power|Class 4 › Buyer power and supplier power]])
- Supplier power is high when suppliers face little competition and you cannot easily make the input yourself. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Buyer power and supplier power|Class 4 › Buyer power and supplier power]])

title: Pricing Game
text: Algorithmic pricing can be used to sustain high prices without explicit agreement, complicating antitrust enforcement.

title: Pricing Game
text:
- Pricing algorithms can learn to sustain high prices without explicit agreement. ([[Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions#Pricing game and algorithmic collusion|Class 8 › Pricing game and algorithmic collusion]])
- Q-learning agents experiment with prices and learn from profits. ([[Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions#Pricing game and algorithmic collusion|Class 8 › Pricing game and algorithmic collusion]])
- This makes antitrust enforcement harder. ([[Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions#Pricing game and algorithmic collusion|Class 8 › Pricing game and algorithmic collusion]])

title: Rivalry
text: Rivalry describes the intensity of competition among current rivals, and price rivalry is a major factor in determining profit.

title: Rivalry
text:
- Price rivalry hurts profit most, while rivalry in quality or brand can be offset by higher prices. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Rivalry|Class 4 › Rivalry]])
- Price rivalry is fierce when products are homogeneous, search costs are low, and switching costs are low. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Rivalry|Class 4 › Rivalry]])
- In the Cola Wars, Coke and Pepsi competed on advertising and marketing instead of a price war. ([[Class 4 - Industry Analysis#Case - Cola Wars|Class 4 › Case - Cola Wars]])

id: vault/Sources/Class 1 - Introduction to Strategy.md#Why strategy is hard#0
title: Class 1 - Introduction to Strategy
text:
Profit is revenue minus cost, so "raise revenue, cut cost" sounds easy. The lecture argued that good strategy is hard for three reasons: decisions can have counterintuitive effects that change outcomes a lot, you have to predict how other players will respond to your choices, and the world is noisy, so you must figure out which few factors actually matter. The two tools for making progress are understanding the context and dissecting the trade-offs.

A warm-up example: a heavy-machinery CEO is offered technology that makes plants easy to repurpose or sell. Flexibility sounds good, but if a potential entrant is watching, being able to walk away easily can weaken your threat to fight entry. This previews the entry-deterrence ideas later in the course.

title: Class 1 - Introduction to Strategy
text:
The same move can be great for one firm and a disaster for another. Context includes who the buyers are, the cost structure, competitors and their interests, legal and regulatory limits, internal incentives, and assets such as brand, location, technology and IP.

Amazon buying Whole Foods (2017) made sense for Amazon but would not for FedEx or Uber: it increased Prime stickiness and gave Amazon shopper data, gave it roughly 500 stores to use as last-mile delivery hubs for Amazon Fresh, and defended against Walmart in physical retail.

M-Pesa succeeded in Kenya because of urban-to-rural remittances, more than 80,000 cash-out agents, light regulation (it was treated as a telecom product, not banking), and Safaricom being the dominant carrier. India looked promising (over 600 million unbanked people, about 900 million mobile subscribers) but differed: mobile money is regulated as banking there, and Vodafone was the number-two carrier, not number one.

id: vault/Sources/Class 1 - Introduction to Strategy.md#Trade-offs and opportunity cost#0
title: Class 1 - Introduction to Strategy
text:
Firms do not control revenue or cost directly; they control operating decisions that move both, usually in opposite directions (higher quality raises willingness to pay but also cost; more volume usually needs lower prices). Examples of trade-offs: Netflix's password-sharing crackdown, Apple's App Tracking Transparency, Disney launching streaming and cannibalizing cable, Starbucks mobile ordering hurting the in-store experience, and Google adding AI answers that may reduce ad clicks.

Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up. Disney gave up more than $300 million a year in licensing fees when it pulled content from Netflix for Disney+.

title: Class 1 - Introduction to Strategy
text:
The lecture quoted Porter (1996): a company can outperform rivals only if it can establish a difference it can preserve. In innovative industries these differences close quickly, so innovation must be continual. Working definition: strategy is a plan of action to achieve the firm's goal (profit) that establishes a persistent difference over rivals, by dissecting context and trade-offs to understand how others will respond and which features of the environment matter.

Bad strategy is different from bad luck: Porsche decided in 2019 to make the next Macan electric-only, then in 2025 added combustion and hybrid versions back, saying it would have made the same call on the data available at the time.

id: vault/Sources/Class 1 - Introduction to Strategy.md#The economic approach#0
title: Class 1 - Introduction to Strategy
text:
Economics frames decisions by identifying decision makers, goals, choices and outputs, then moving from describe to predict to prescribe. Decision makers include rivals, suppliers, regulators and start-ups, not just your own executives. Firms are assumed to maximize profit. Use economic costs rather than accounting costs: ignore sunk costs and include opportunity costs.

Equilibrium is the "rest point" of a system: environmental changes create threats and opportunities, which drive entry and exit, and competition pushes the market back toward equilibrium.

title: Class 1 - Introduction to Strategy
text: The Oakland A's had a small payroll compared with rich teams. Scouts valued players partly on looks (the "Good Face"). The A's found that on-base percentage predicted wins better than slugging, yet sluggers were paid far more, which was an arbitrage opportunity for cheap wins. Around 2000, wins from OBP were much cheaper than wins from slugging; by about 2004-2005 the market price and the true value of OBP had converged. Lessons: the A's found a way to lower the cost of wins, but markets move toward equilibrium, so the advantage did not last.

id: vault/Sources/Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture.md#Profit maximization as the goal#0
title: Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture
text:
Why assume firms maximize profit? A firm that ignores profit goes bankrupt, cannot fund the investments it needs, and gets its assets redeployed by the capital market (for example through a takeover). Long-run profit maximization is not quarterly earnings management, short-run exploitation of employees, suppliers or customers, or unethical shortcuts.

Social impact: for firms whose customers value it, social impact is part of the value proposition, so long-run profit and social impact line up. For firms whose customers do not value it, competition makes costly social goals hard to sustain, and regulation is needed to level the field. Large institutional shareholders can push managers either because they have pro-social preferences or because they believe it raises long-run profits. The course tools also apply to non-profits: how to best reach a social objective with limited resources.

"Maximize profit" is a goal, not a strategy, in the same way "win" is a coach's goal. Strategy is the set of decisions (inputs, processes, products, customers, prices) that lead to long-run profit.

id: vault/Sources/Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture.md#The profit function#0
title: Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture
text: Profit = (price - cost per unit) x quantity. A strategy raises profit only by raising price, lowering unit cost, or raising quantity. The levers interact: H&H Bail Bonds tried to raise quantity by loosening standards, but that also raised costs.

id: vault/Sources/Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture.md#Value created and value captured#0
title: Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture
text:
Value created is the gap between the customer's benefit (willingness to pay, B) and the cost (C). The price P splits it: B - P is consumer surplus and P - C is the firm's profit. A firm must create value before it can capture it.

To create more value a firm can increase benefits, decrease costs, or increase quantity (new markets, new customers, more usage). Examples: Amazon and IKEA lower cost; Uber and Spotify raise benefit; pharmaceutical firms find new patient groups.

Jay-Z moved his music exclusively to Tidal in 2017 (about 3 million paying users) and returned to Spotify (about 113 million paying users) in 2019. Owning the whole pie mattered less than the pie being much smaller: a smaller slice of a bigger pie can be more.

Allbirds used sustainable materials, which raised willingness to pay only for sustainability-minded buyers while raising cost for all, so other buyers went elsewhere; it later closed its stores to focus on e-commerce.

id: vault/Sources/Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture.md#Why firms fail to capture value#0
title: Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture
section: Why firms fail to capture value
text:
Creating value does not guarantee profit. Firms fail to capture value if they do not really create value, if the party that benefits is not the party that pays, or if competition drives prices down. They capture more by being irreplaceable and by innovating on pricing or revenue models.

Netflix's 2023 password-sharing crackdown was a bet that shared users would buy their own accounts rather than quit (costs up a little, benefit down a little, quantity up a lot). Game studios adding NFTs in 2022 angered players, a drop in benefit, echoing Blizzard's Diablo III auction house in 2013.

id: vault/Sources/Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture.md#Astroscale and public goods#0
title: Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture
text: Space debris in low earth orbit (tens of millions of pieces moving around 17,000 mph) causes collisions, and each collision creates more debris. Cleaning it up is hard for practical reasons (small, fast, hard to see), legal reasons (the launching country owns each object) and economic reasons: debris is a negative externality and cleanup is a public good, non-rival and non-excludable. Astroscale's ELSA satellite uses an adhesive plate to catch debris and steer it into the atmosphere. Its revenue plan: sell mapping data, contract with satellite operators to remove their own dead satellites (a private good), and eventually be paid for general cleanup by a party like NASA or a consortium.

id: vault/Sources/Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture.md#Case - CF Industries#0
title: Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture
text: CF sells nitrogen fertilizer, a commodity, yet was very profitable. Fertilizer's value depends on being in the right place in a window of a few weeks. CF created value by having ammonia where and when farmers needed it: 29 storage terminals across the Midwest (it rents storage at about $150 per ton), multiple transport modes including about 5,000 owned or leased rail cars, and demand forecasting. It lowered cost thanks to cheap natural gas (70-80% of ammonia production cost), running expensive plants (about $1 billion each) with minimal downtime, and preventive maintenance.

id: vault/Sources/Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture.md#Case - CF Industries#1
title: Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture
text: CF captured value through its terminals: ammonia is hazardous and needs special storage, new terminals are heavily restricted by regulation (an entry barrier), and storage lets CF sell to the higher-priced agricultural market rather than the industrial market, which paid $150-200 less per ton. That is why it acquired Terra. It also captured value through better pricing information and pricing innovation (forward sales hedged with natural gas swaps, and "summer fill" programs that price discriminate between farmers with and without storage). Its $3.8 billion expansion led Agrium, Yara and Mosaic to cancel their own plans, a form of entry deterrence.

id: vault/Sources/Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability.md#Irreplaceability drives value capture#0
title: Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability
text: How much value a firm captures depends on the price it can charge. If nobody else can do what you do, customers have no easy alternative and you can price well above cost. If many firms can do it, customers choose on price and competition pushes price toward cost. Irreplaceability is not the only reason firms fail to capture value, but it is the most common one.

id: vault/Sources/Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability.md#Defining added value#0
title: Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability
text:
Added value = total value created with you in the market minus total value created without you. Put differently: how much would everyone else together pay to keep you in? A player should not expect to get more than its added value, because the others would be better off letting it walk away and splitting what remains.

Capacity shows how added value moves. Before the AI boom, DRAM makers were easy to replace (a buyer who skipped Samsung bought Micron), so prices were low and SK Hynix lost money in 2023. With AI demand, capacity is tight: OpenAI's projected need of up to 900,000 DRAM wafers a month is more than double the industry's HBM capacity, so each supplier is hard to replace and profits jumped. Red Sea attacks in 2025 forced rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope, straining shipping capacity and raising profits for carriers like Maersk.

id: vault/Sources/Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability.md#Joint venture exercise#0
title: Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability
text:
Three firms can form partnerships with these profits: all three together $100M; A and B $80M; A and C $70M; B and C $40M; any firm alone $15M.

The three-firm venture creates the most value. Added values: A = 100 - 40 = $60M; B = 100 - 70 = $30M; C = 100 - 80 = $20M.

Upper bound: a firm should get at most its added value. If A took more than $60M, B and C would get less than the $40M they can earn alone and would leave.

Lower bound: a firm should get at least its outside option (BATNA), here $15M, and more when the others have low added value. A should get no less than 100 - (30 + 20) = $50M, so A's predicted share is between $50M and $60M.

Key principles: raise your own added value, raise your outside option, and lower other players' added value to improve your negotiating position.

id: vault/Sources/Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability.md#Examples of shifting added value#0
title: Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability
text:
Apple and OLED screens: before 2018 Samsung was the only firm able to make OLED screens at iPhone X size in enough volume; the display was $97 of the phone's $376 production cost. Apple got LG to start making OLED phone screens, and Samsung lost its irreplaceability.

Australia's News Media Bargaining Code (2021) tried to make Google and Facebook pay news outlets. Google threatened to pull search and Facebook briefly blocked news, but both eventually paid, around $1 billion in total. When the three-year deals expired, Meta said it would not renew and would remove news rather than be designated under the code.

id: vault/Sources/Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability.md#Case - Intel#0
title: Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability
text:
In DRAM, Intel's 1972 strategy was innovation and product design, being first to market, pricing high and moving on. That fit a new market where innovation mattered more than scale. By 1979 the market grew fast, product cycles shrank, scale mattered more, and Japanese producers with better manufacturing entered. Intel's added value in DRAM collapsed, so it moved to a market that fit its strengths: microprocessors. Lessons from DRAM: protect IP, commodities are hard to profit from, and manufacturing yield matters.

In the early PC years IBM was the most irreplaceable player thanks to its mainframe reputation ("nobody ever got fired for buying IBM"), which let it set the architecture standard. IBM's open model brought many partners and growth but lower margins and less control; Apple's closed model kept margin and control but grew slower.

id: vault/Sources/Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability.md#Case - Intel#1
title: Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability
text:
By the 1990s the power had shifted to Intel and Microsoft ("Wintel"). The reason was network effects: apps are written for an OS, the OS talks to the processor, users go where the apps are, and developers go where the users are. Unlike a hard drive, you cannot swap out the OS or processor without breaking the apps. Watershed events: Compaq reverse-engineered the BIOS, so compatibility required Intel rather than IBM, and IBM delayed the 386 while it pushed its proprietary PS/2 and OS/2, so the market moved on without it. Intel's customers said they would need more than a 2x performance gap before switching to RISC.

Intel captured its added value through Intel Inside (co-op ad money that PC makers could not refuse, a prisoner's dilemma that commoditized them), a systems business that showed PC makers they were replaceable, rationing new chips by past sales to discourage switching to AMD, and IP lawsuits against AMD.

id: vault/Sources/Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability.md#Case - Intel#2
title: Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability
text: In 2018 Intel had little added value in modem chips (Qualcomm owned the IP and was faster), but Apple used Intel modems in half its phones during a royalty dispute, which shifted bargaining power from Qualcomm to Apple.

title: Class 3 - Added Value and Irreplaceability
text: Being irreplaceable is key to capturing value, and added value measures irreplaceability. Intel's added value vanished in DRAM but persisted in microprocessors because network effects locked in developers and users. The lecture closed by asking what NVIDIA is trying to do with CUDA.

id: vault/Sources/Class 4 - Industry Analysis.md#Five Forces as a starting point#0
title: Class 4 - Industry Analysis
section: Five Forces as a starting point
text: Porter's Five Forces asks how much value an industry can create and how much of it firms can keep as profit. It is a checklist, not an answer: it makes sure you have covered the parts of the context that matter, but it does not tell you what to do. The five forces are substitutes, buyer power, supplier power, entry, and rivalry. Later classes on competitive advantage ask why some firms in an industry earn more than others.

title: Class 4 - Industry Analysis
text: A substitute meets the same need as your product. Its effect on profit is similar to an entrant with a different product. Which products count as substitutes depends on context.

id: vault/Sources/Class 4 - Industry Analysis.md#Buyer power and supplier power#0
title: Class 4 - Industry Analysis
text:
Buyers can push prices down when they are few and large, when there are many substitutes for your product, and when they could easily bypass you or make the product themselves. Supplier power is buyer power turned around: suppliers extract high prices when they face little competition, have few substitutes, and when you cannot easily make the input yourself.

Beef example: ranchers used to get about 50 cents of each retail beef dollar; in 2021 they got 37 cents, even with record retail prices. The four largest meatpackers (Tyson, Cargill, National Beef and JBS) grew from 36% to 85% market share since the 1980s, cut capacity during the pandemic, and buy through private contracts with feedlots, which reduces price transparency.

id: vault/Sources/Class 4 - Industry Analysis.md#Entry and barriers to entry#0
title: Class 4 - Industry Analysis
text:
Profitable industries attract entrants and imitators, which lowers prices and splits profit, so the entry force looks at potential rivals, not just current ones. Barriers to entry make a market hard to enter or less profitable for entrants than incumbents. Barriers include economies of scale relative to market size, scarce resources (a good location, access to inputs or distribution), learning curves, network effects, and intellectual property.

Minimum efficient scale (MES) is the smallest output that reaches minimum unit cost. The ratio of MES to industry demand gives the maximum number of efficient firms: cement has few plants, dry cleaning has many.

A direct network effect means each user values the product more as more people use it (languages, phones, social media). An indirect or platform network effect means one type of user benefits from more users of another type (buyers and sellers).

IP matters a lot in pharmaceuticals: once a drug is on the market it can be reverse engineered, so billions in R&D need enforceable patents.

title: Class 4 - Industry Analysis
text: Rivalry is how intensely current rivals compete. Price rivalry hurts profit most; rivalry in quality or brand can be offset by higher prices. Price rivalry is fierce when small price cuts win many sales: homogeneous products, low search costs, low switching costs, low brand loyalty, many sellers, frequent purchases, high fixed costs, and excess capacity.

title: Class 4 - Industry Analysis
text:
Rivalry: fueling has always been low margin (gas stations earn most from their convenience stores), and electricity is hard to differentiate except by location and charging speed. Entry and substitutes: a chicken-and-egg problem between cars and chargers, and home charging, which is about 80% of EV charging. Buyer power: switching between networks is easy (Tesla was the exception), and density cuts both ways. Supplier power: landowners with good sites, slow and costly grid connections, and expensive equipment. Business models: sell equipment (ChargePoint), own chargers and charge per use (EVgo), advertising screens (Volta), or a restaurant model.

By December 2023 shares had fallen about 70% for ChargePoint, 67% for Blink and 20% for EVgo. By October 2025 the network had matured: fast-charging ports rose more than 80% in two years to over 60,300, and failed charging visits fell to 14%, just as the $7,500 federal EV tax credit expired.

title: Class 4 - Industry Analysis
text: Carbonated soft drinks are about 27% of US beverage consumption and $48 billion in US sales. Coke and Pepsi hold about 70% of the market, and concentrate producers earn gross profit around 83% of net sales, versus 25-35% for an average US firm.

title: Class 4 - Industry Analysis
text: Five Forces: substitutes are everywhere (water, coffee, juice, beer), but Coke kept its product "within arm's reach of desire." Buyer power ranges from low to high; profitability for concentrate producers ranks vending > convenience stores > grocery > fountain. Supplier power is low: concentrate costs about $0.11 per case and inputs are commodities. Rivalry: the two colas are nearly identical, so a price war would be ruinous; instead they compete on advertising and marketing (about 39% of net sales versus about 10% for an average firm) and on new flavors, moving competition from price to dimensions that grow the market. They fight harder abroad, where Pepsi is often a small entrant. Entry barriers: scale in distribution and marketing, established channels, limited shelf space, and brand; a concentrate plant costs only a few million dollars, so plant cost itself is not the barrier.

title: Class 4 - Industry Analysis
text: The cola industry is profitable because buyers and suppliers are weak and entry barriers are high, and Coke and Pepsi shaped competition by creating perceived differentiation. The Five Forces focus on splitting a fixed pie and leave out joint value creation, such as legally growing the market together. If the forces say an industry is attractive, ask why more firms have not entered: either entry is hard or the industry has changed.

title: Class 5 - Competitive Advantage
text:
Competitive advantage is the ability to be consistently more profitable than competitors in the same market or industry. Earlier classes covered value creation and capture and which industries allow long-run profit (Five Forces); this class asks how some firms in an industry create and capture value better than others.

Competitive advantage makes a firm irreplaceable, but not every irreplaceable firm has a competitive advantage. DRAM makers or shipping lines are irreplaceable when capacity is tight, yet they are all roughly the same. A firm with a competitive advantage is irreplaceable in a way that differs from its rivals, so you have to compare it to other firms doing something else and think about what entrants will do.

title: Class 5 - Competitive Advantage
text: Firms in the same industry create value in different ways: Toyota (high-volume, reliable, practical cars) versus Porsche (low-volume, performance, distinctive styling); Uniqlo (quality basics with little style variety) versus Zara (fast-changing trend items); Apple (integrated hardware and software, ease of use, design) versus Microsoft (software with broad compatibility across third-party hardware). A value proposition is a short, precise statement of how the firm intends to create value, its plan for opening the gap between benefit B and cost C.

title: Class 5 - Competitive Advantage
text:
Assets, Activities, Advantage: assets enable activities, and activities create competitive advantage when they fit the context.
- Assets are what the firm has: resources (equipment, location, brand, IP, people, knowledge) and capabilities (developing products, managing customers, procurement, inventory control, motivating staff). Today's assets come from past choices.
- Activities are what the firm chooses to do with its assets. Strategy lives in the activities; the value proposition summarizes them.
- Advantage results when the activities suit the context.

title: Class 5 - Competitive Advantage
text:
Roche example: Roche focused on low-volume conditions (cancer, AIDS, transplantation) and biotech drugs rather than blockbuster pills. Each dose costs hundreds or thousands of dollars, it needs only a small sales force (about 1,600 marketers versus 9,000 at Glaxo and 11,000 at Pfizer) because it sells to specialists, and biotech drugs are harder to copy. The assets it needs are scientific "finders" who can spot promising biotech partners and expertise in clinical trials. Its advantage is in commercializing science that others discover.

Netflix and advertising: in 2020 Reed Hastings said Netflix would not sell ads, because Google, Amazon and Facebook had far better data assets, so Netflix would be strategically disadvantaged. Netflix launched an ad tier in 2022 and in 2024 announced its own ad-tech platform once it had invested in the needed assets.

id: vault/Sources/Class 5 - Competitive Advantage.md#Three sources of competitive advantage#0
title: Class 5 - Competitive Advantage
text:
The sources mirror the ways to create value: benefit-based, cost-based, and niche (quantity)-based.

Cost-based: Chevron used sensors and machine learning for predictive maintenance on about 5,000 heat exchangers, saving millions. Porter argues operational excellence alone is not a competitive advantage, but it could be one if Chevron has more or better data or gets ahead and stays ahead. AMD under Lisa Su bet on PC and server CPUs and graphics when conventional wisdom favored mobile, paid $325 million to exit its contract with GlobalFoundries so TSMC could make its chips, and invested in graphics despite NVIDIA.

Benefit-based: Johnson & Johnson's brand certified quality for commodity products like children's Tylenol; the premium over the store brand was about 50% in 2019 ($7.49 versus $4.99). Supporting that brand required top-quality manufacturing and transparency. Around 2010, weak quality control, cost cutting and a "phantom recall" damaged the brand and pushed shoppers to generics.

id: vault/Sources/Class 5 - Competitive Advantage.md#Three sources of competitive advantage#1
title: Class 5 - Competitive Advantage
text:
Niche-based: find a subset of customers where price rivalry is reduced, protected by a barrier to entry. Horizontal differentiation means customers disagree about the ideal product (music, fashion, cars). Vertical differentiation means customers agree which product is better but differ in how much they will pay for quality. Kam Pek Casino in Macau targets low rollers; since Macau dealers are expensive (1.8% unemployment, local-hire rules), it uses live dealers on video so 8 dealers serve 900 gamblers instead of 100 dealers, keeping labor cost 30% below other casinos. Dell sold direct to knowledgeable corporate buyers, skipping reseller markups; IBM tried to copy it but angered its resellers and its manufacturing was built for standard products.

Casper shows the limit: bed-in-a-box grew fast, but dozens of copycats entered because there was no entry barrier, and Casper never became profitable. Bombas used buy-one-give-one; TOMS lost its edge when rivals copied the model, and Warby Parker scaled its donations back because giving away identical products is costly.

title: Class 5 - Competitive Advantage
text:
Enterprise was consistently the most profitable US rental car company. Its choices reinforce each other:
- Locations: it served people who are not traveling and skipped the crowded airport market, opening many small, convenient, low-cost offices; about 90% of the US population lives within 15 minutes of one.
- Referrals: close relationships with body shops and insurers, integrated through its ARMS/ECARS systems, with staff placed at insurers. Insurers pay for the rental, so Enterprise competes on service rather than price.
- Organization: hires sociable college graduates, pays for performance tied to branch profit, promotes from within; runs its own reservation and inventory systems and sells used cars through about 30 lots.

Locations justify referrals, referrals justify locations, and the organization sustains both, which creates a chicken-and-egg problem for Avis or Hertz trying to copy it. One risk is that promote-from-within needs constant growth.

id: vault/Sources/Class 6 - Entry and Positioning.md#Facts about entry and exit#0
title: Class 6 - Entry and Positioning
text: Entry and exit are pervasive; entrants and exiting firms tend to be smaller than established firms; most entrants do not survive 10 years, but those that survive grow quickly; and entry and exit rates vary by industry. Implications: plan for an unknown future competitor, expect most new ventures to fail, and know how important entry is in your own industry. Entry is broader than new firms: it includes new markets (M-Pesa entering India, Amazon entering grocery) and new products (Ozempic, Vanilla Coke, the microprocessor).

title: Class 6 - Entry and Positioning
text: An entrant has to choose a position: a price and a bundle of features. When you enter you take customers from incumbents, and incumbents may react. Counter-positioning means choosing a position the incumbent does not want to fight, because fighting would cost it too much with its existing customers.

id: vault/Sources/Class 6 - Entry and Positioning.md#Water bottle exercise#0
title: Class 6 - Entry and Positioning
text:
Two products: a high-quality insulated bottle (marginal cost $10, every customer values it at $20) and a low-quality plastic bottle (marginal cost $5). There are 10 customers: 2 value the plastic bottle at $15 and 8 value it at $10. A monopolist would sell the insulated bottle at $20 to all 10 for a profit of $100.

Now an incumbent sells the insulated bottle at $20 and you enter:
- Copy the insulated bottle at $19: the incumbent undercuts to $18.99, which leads toward a price war. Direct attack invites retaliation.
- Plastic bottle at $14 (only $1 of surplus to the 2 high-value customers): retaliating by cutting to $18.99 earns the incumbent $90 versus $80 from accommodating, so it retaliates.
- Plastic bottle at $11 (gives those 2 customers $4 of surplus): winning them back needs a price of $15.99, which earns $60 versus $80 from accommodating, so the incumbent accommodates and you earn $12.
- Below $10 you would attract everyone, so retaliation is certain.

id: vault/Sources/Class 6 - Entry and Positioning.md#Water bottle exercise#1
title: Class 6 - Entry and Positioning
text: Intuition: to win back a few customers the incumbent must lower its price to all of them. Target a small segment and price low enough that fighting is not worth it. If the targeted segment is larger, you must price lower; if it is smaller, you can price higher. Counter-positioning works better when the incumbent would find it hard to make your product well.

title: Class 6 - Entry and Positioning
text:
- Southwest positioned against driving, using secondary airports, point-to-point routes and one aircraft type. Rivals mostly accommodated by retreating to long-haul and business routes.
- Warby Parker sold prescription glasses at $95 direct to consumers, bypassing Luxottica. Luxottica could not match the price without cannibalizing its own stores and licensing business, so it accommodated.
- Google Docs (2006) entered as a low-end alternative; Microsoft responded with Office 365 in 2011 and sped it up from 2014.
- Perplexity attacked Google Search directly with an answer engine. Google retaliated with AI Overviews from 2024, even though they reduce ad clicks.
- Mounjaro (Eli Lilly) arrived five years after Ozempic (Novo Nordisk) and gained share on better outcomes.
- SpaceX entered space launch after Boeing and Lockheed Martin formed the United Launch Alliance in 2006; Falcon 9 was certified for national security launches in 2015.

title: Class 6 - Entry and Positioning
text:
The Model S was Tesla's first real production car (about 10,000 a year) and the first entry by a new US carmaker since WWII. In H1 2013 regulatory ZEV credits were 12% of Tesla's revenue; without them its operating margin was -16%, against BMW's +11% in 2012. The lecture showed that learning-curve and scale effects could make the numbers much better than they looked for a start-up.

Barriers in autos were high: brand and advertising (Ford spends about $4 billion a year), plants costing billions with MES of 100,000-250,000 cars, about 1,000 suppliers per model, large dealer networks (Toyota about 1,600 US dealers; Ford and GM about 4,000), and years of design capability. Tesla got around them: the Roadster built its brand; it bought the Fremont factory for $42 million; EVs are simpler (far fewer engine parts, no transmission, no cooling system), so fewer suppliers and capabilities were needed; it partnered with Lotus and Panasonic early; and it sold directly instead of through dealers.

title: Class 6 - Entry and Positioning
text: Musk's 2006 "master plan" was to start at the high end, where customers pay a premium, and move down-market with each model. Takeaways: exploit a wave of change and incumbents' inertia; sequence positions and capabilities; start at the high end where nobody has scale. Tesla's durable advantage may lie in software, batteries and charging rather than car making. In 2025 GM sold about 170,000 EVs versus Tesla's 1.64 million. Later entrants: Rivian (adventure lifestyle plus a 100,000-van order from Amazon) and Lucid (luxury, above Tesla, funded by a Saudi fund).

id: vault/Sources/Class 7 - Entry Dynamics.md#Case - Ryanair, first entry#0
title: Class 7 - Entry Dynamics
text: Before deregulation, European aviation was run by national flag carriers acting like regulated monopolies that colluded with each other, and they were inefficient. British Airways moved 308 passengers per staff member in 1978 and 483 in 1985, versus 708 for US airlines in 1978, and flew at 60-70% utilization. As the industry deregulated, the Dublin-London route was very profitable. Deregulation made it a contestable market: if an incumbent earns a lot on a route, someone can enter.

id: vault/Sources/Class 7 - Entry Dynamics.md#Case - Ryanair, first entry#1
title: Class 7 - Entry Dynamics
text: Ryanair entered with turboprops between Luton and Dublin at a £98 fare, promising to be more efficient. Its planes could carry only about 64,000 of the route's 500,000 passengers. In a simple short-run calculation, Aer Lingus and British Airways would earn about £60M by accommodating (keeping the £166 fare and losing 64,000 passengers) versus about £34.5M by retaliating (cutting to £98 to keep everyone). But the incumbents expected Ryanair to expand (it had applied to fly jets, and £98 was probably not sustainable, since costs were likely above £95-100). They retaliated harshly and Ryanair nearly went bankrupt.

id: vault/Sources/Class 7 - Entry Dynamics.md#Case - Ryanair, second entry#0
title: Class 7 - Entry Dynamics
text: After near-bankruptcy Ryanair repositioned as a true no-frills, low-cost airline: secondary destinations, a standard fleet, staff paid on productivity and sales, extra fees for almost everything, and skimping on everything except maintenance. It advertised the bare-bones experience openly. The first attempt was an undifferentiated direct attack with a murky target customer and drew retaliation; the second focused on very price-sensitive travelers with an offer incumbents could not match and did not want to, because they kept their other customers. This is counter-positioning.

title: Class 7 - Entry Dynamics
text:
An entry game is a structured way to think about how an incumbent will respond. The entrant chooses to enter or stay out; the incumbent chooses to retaliate or accommodate. You solve it by looking forward and reasoning backward (backward induction).

In the basic Ryanair game the incumbent gets £69M if there is no entry, £60M if it accommodates and £34M if it retaliates, so it accommodates, and the entrant enters if its fixed cost F is below £4.4M.

Add a second stage where, after accommodation, the entrant can enter another of the incumbent's markets (entrant £40M - F, incumbent £30M). Now the entrant would surely expand, so the incumbent compares £34M (retaliate) with £30M (accommodate then lose the second market) and retaliates. Knowing that, the entrant stays out. The counterintuitive lesson: having the extra option to expand makes the entrant worse off, because it triggers retaliation. The entrant would remove that option if it could.

A threat to retaliate works only if it is credible: when the moment comes, the incumbent must actually want to carry it out.

title: Class 7 - Entry Dynamics
text:
The US shale boom after 2008 (fracking plus horizontal drilling) raised US oil output. At its November 2014 meeting OPEC chose not to cut production, pushing prices down to squeeze shale producers. The threat was not credible for long: Saudi Arabia needed about $106 a barrel to balance its budget while oil was near $45. Shale kept improving its efficiency, OPEC backed down in 2016, and by 2017 shale was a low-cost technology. Many small shale producers also meant OPEC could not punish each one.

Complications for entry games: irrational incumbents that fight out of ego or culture, uncertainty about the incumbent's payoffs, and multiple entrants.

title: Class 7 - Entry Dynamics
text:
Keeping competitors out almost always pays. Incumbents change the payoffs before entry happens:
1. Limit pricing: price low to make entry unattractive (Alcoa).
2. Capacity expansion: add capacity to commit to fighting (DuPont in titanium dioxide, CF Industries).
3. Product proliferation: fill every niche so there is no room (cereal, drug variants, railroad branch lines).
4. Predatory pricing to build a reputation (OPEC, Uber, Walmart).

Deterrence works only if the commitment is public and made before the entrant invests. In the 1905 North Dakota railroad war, the Great Northern tried to block the Soo Line; by 1912 the region had 13 branch lines, one per 24 miles, instead of 10, one per 85 miles.

id: vault/Sources/Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions.md#Case - Bitter Competition, the setup#0
title: Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions
text:
The case is about aspartame. NutraSweet (owned by Monsanto) held the patent, which expired in Europe and Canada in 1987 and in the US in 1992, giving a two-stage game. Minimum efficient scale was large (about 2,000 tons) compared with total demand (about 6,000 tons in 1986), and European demand was below one efficient plant. Buyers were concentrated: Coke and Pepsi bought about half. Safety regulation slowed rival sweeteners, and NutraSweet co-branded with its customers.

NutraSweet tried to stretch its patent with long-term exclusive contracts and ingredient branding (the swirl logo on cans). It charged about $70/lb, or $50/lb to Coke and Pepsi, against an estimated marginal cost of about $18/lb.

The entrant, Holland Sweetener Company (HSC), targeted buyers who wanted cheaper, possibly unbranded, aspartame. It was unlikely to be more efficient: it entered Europe at only 500 tons, below MES and low on the learning curve, with an estimated marginal cost of about $30/lb. The gap between $30 and $70 looked attractive, but NutraSweet had lower cost, a stronger brand and deep pockets.

id: vault/Sources/Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions.md#What happened#0
title: Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions
text:
NutraSweet retaliated in Europe: prices fell to about $22/lb, below HSC's marginal cost, and several other firms exited. HSC filed EU complaints about abuse of dominant position (NutraSweet's exclusive contracts with Coke and Pepsi ran to 1990) and dumping; the European Commission sided with HSC and imposed a $15/lb duty on NutraSweet. NutraSweet then committed to fight by planning a 2,000-ton plant in France and doubling its Augusta plant, and alternative sweeteners stalled in regulation, which raised the value of retaliating.

The US market was far larger (about 8,000 tons versus 1,400 in Europe). HSC expanded to 2,000 tons and entered the US about a year after the patent expired, which gave NutraSweet hundreds of millions in extra profit. Then Coke and Pepsi signed near-exclusive long-term deals with NutraSweet. They were the real winners: HSC's presence as an outside option let them push NutraSweet's price down from $50/lb, worth roughly $200M a year, about all of their US demand.

id: vault/Sources/Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions.md#HSC's major mistake#0
title: Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions
text:
HSC created $400-600M of value for Coke and Pepsi but captured little of it. It believed Coke and Pepsi wanted it around, which was true, but once HSC had built its plant, they used it as leverage and then stayed with NutraSweet. HSC needed a credible commitment, a written purchase agreement signed before it built the plant. In game form: if Coke and Pepsi cannot commit, they will buy only from NutraSweet once HSC has entered, so HSC should not enter; with a binding commitment, HSC should enter, and Coke and Pepsi would benefit from signing it.

Market structure drove the case: high MES (with tiny MES, anyone could pick off small customers), Coke and Pepsi's large share, their reluctance to switch because of branding and safety, and delays to other sweeteners.

id: vault/Sources/Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions.md#Repeated interactions and reputation#0
title: Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions
text:
Firms often interact for years (Coke and Pepsi, Intel and AMD, airlines). Repetition lets players build a reputation and cooperate by threatening retaliation.

One long-term player facing many short-term players can build a reputation for retaliating, because each short-term player will not be around to benefit from breaking it. Walmart's policy of fighting every lawsuit in court is costly each time, but no single plaintiff gains from challenging it.

Two long-term players can sustain cooperation. Haagen-Dazs and Ben & Jerry's seem to split the super-premium ice cream market into smooth and chunky flavors; when one crossed into the other's territory, a price war followed, so each stays out. Anheuser-Busch used a "trigger strategy" in beer: when Miller and Coors cut prices in 1988, it slashed prices on Bud in key markets, and the rivals quickly stopped.

id: vault/Sources/Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions.md#Pricing game and algorithmic collusion#0
title: Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions
text:
In an in-class pricing game, teams set prices each round against three rivals. A chat was then added, first unrestricted and then with price fixing forbidden and an "AI antitrust authority" that would fine violators four times their last five rounds of profit plus an 80% profit cut for five rounds.

Pricing algorithms, including Q-learning agents that experiment with prices and learn from profits, can learn to sustain high prices without explicit agreement, which makes antitrust enforcement harder.

title: Class 8 - Strategic and Repeated Interactions
text: Large incumbents expand capacity to deter entrants, slow entrants down while they are learning, lock large customers into long-term contracts, and punish small entrants to send a message. When incumbents cannot drive each other out, they may collude through repeated interaction, which regulators try to prevent.

title: Economic Approach
text: Economics frames decisions by identifying decision makers, goals, choices, and outputs, moving from description to prediction to prescription.

text:

title: Profit Function
text: Profit is calculated as (price - cost per unit) multiplied by the quantity sold. Strategies aim to raise profit by changing price, cost, or quantity.

title: Strategic Context
text: The context includes various factors like buyers, competitors, legal limits, and internal assets that influence outcomes.

title: Strategic Context
text:

title: Strategy
text: Strategy is a plan to achieve a firm's goal by establishing a persistent difference over rivals.

title: Strategy
text:

- Astroscale plans to sell mapping data and contract for satellite removal to fund general cleanup. ([[Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture#Astroscale and public goods|Class 2 › Astroscale and public goods]])

title: Value Creation
text: Value created is the gap between a customer's benefit and the cost. Firms must create this value before they can capture it.

title: Value Creation
text:
- Value created is the gap between the customer's benefit (willingness to pay, B) and the cost (C). ([[Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture#Value created and value captured|Class 2 › Value created and value captured]])
- Firms can increase value by increasing benefits, decreasing costs, or increasing quantity. ([[Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture#Value created and value captured|Class 2 › Value created and value captured]])
- A smaller slice of a bigger pie can be more valuable. ([[Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture#Value created and value captured|Class 2 › Value created and value captured]])
- Allbirds raised willingness to pay only for sustainability-minded buyers while raising cost for all. ([[Class 2 - Value Creation and Capture#Value created and value captured|Class 2 › Value created and value captured]])

title: Value Proposition
text: The value proposition is a statement detailing how a firm intends to create value and bridge the gap between customer benefits and costs.

title: Value Proposition
text:
- Firms create value in different ways, such as Toyota focusing on volume and reliability versus Porsche focusing on performance. ([[Class 5 - Competitive Advantage#Value proposition|Class 5 › Value proposition]])
- The value proposition outlines the plan for opening the gap between benefit B and cost C. ([[Class 5 - Competitive Advantage#Value proposition|Class 5 › Value proposition]])
